match.reason: The closest bank point, Variation in populations, teaches how to calculate allele frequency but never defines the gene pool or says that evolution is a change in allele frequencies over time, so it is related rather than the same idea.

draft.title: The gene pool
card: A population is a group of the same species living in the same area. Its gene pool is all the alleles of all its genes, carried by every individual in it.
Allele frequency is how common one allele is in the gene pool. It is the number of copies of that allele divided by the total copies of that gene, often given as a fraction or percentage.
Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population's gene pool over generations. One individual's alleles stay the same during its life, so a single individual does not evolve.
If the allele frequencies stay the same from one generation to the next, the gene pool has not changed and no evolution has happened.
draft.remember: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population over generations.

a.q: Which observation shows that a population has evolved?
opts: The frequency of an allele has changed over generations
One animal has grown larger during its life
The population has more individuals than before
Each individual still carries the same alleles
a.why: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in the gene pool over generations. A bigger population does not by itself mean allele frequencies changed, and an animal growing is not a change in the gene pool.
a.clue: Look for a change in the gene pool, not in one body or in numbers.

b.q: In a population of 50 beetles, each carries two copies of a colour gene. There are 40 copies of the allele G and 60 copies of the allele g. What is the frequency of g in the gene pool?
opts: 0.6, as 60 of the 100 gene copies are g
0.4, as 40 of the 100 gene copies are G
0.3, as 60 copies are shared across 50 beetles
0.5, as both alleles are present in the population
b.why: The gene pool has 50 × 2 = 100 copies of the gene. The allele g makes up 60 of them, so its frequency is 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6. The value 0.4 is the frequency of G, the other allele.
b.clue: Count gene copies, not beetles. Each beetle has two.

a.best: The frequency of an allele has changed over generations

b.best: 0.6, as 60 of the 100 gene copies are g

problems.detail: The distractor '0.3, as 60 copies are shared across 50 beetles' has reasoning that does not produce its number (60 ÷ 50 is 1.2, not 0.3). This may confuse students. A coherent miscount, such as 60 ÷ 200 = 0.3 from counting four copies per beetle, would make a fairer distractor.
